argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0107d: meeting "d" (detailed design) of series SY0107.

PROJECT
The team is designing a voice-controlled kitchen timer.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  Industrial Designer (ID)  Rafael  present
B  Marketing Expert (ME)  Nadia  present
C  User Interface designer (UI)  Tomasz  present
D  Project Manager (PM)  Helen  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0107a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kickoff meeting, the team members introduced themselves, and the project manager presented the project: a voice-controlled kitchen timer that is original, trendy and user-friendly and can be operated hands-free while cooking. The team tried out the whiteboard by drawing their favourite kitchen gadgets. The project manager presented the budget: a selling price of 25 euros, a maximum production cost of 12.50 euros per unit, and a profit target of 50 million euros. In a first round of ideas, the team agreed the timer should support multiple simultaneous timers and use a wake word, and discussed kitchen noise, a backup button, a phone app and a fridge magnet without settling them. The project manager assigned individual preparation tasks for the functional design meeting, which follows in about thirty minutes.
  decisions: The timer will support more than one timer running at a time; the exact number is still to be determined. The timer will use a wake word.
  actions: The industrial designer will work on the working design, including what microphones are affordable. The user interface designer will work on the technical functions design. The marketing expert will work on user requirements, including research on what home cooks want from a kitchen timer. The project manager will write up and distribute the minutes.
  problems: Kitchen noise may stop the timer from hearing users, and a good microphone adds cost within the 12.50 euro limit. Whether to add a backup button for loud situations was left open. A phone app connection was parked as probably too expensive. A fridge magnet or stand was left for the conceptual design meeting. The number of simultaneous timers is undecided. The target group is broadly defined as home cooks.
  action item SY0107a.ai1: Work on the working design (components), including researching affordable microphones (owner A, active)
  action item SY0107a.ai2: Work on the technical functions design, including how people talk to the timer (owner C, active)
  action item SY0107a.ai3: Work on user requirements, including research on what home cooks want from a kitchen timer (owner B, active)
  action item SY0107a.ai4: Write up the meeting minutes and send them to the team (owner D, active)
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested three or four named timers that announce which one is done.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested a backup button for when it is too loud; it was left undecided.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested connecting the timer to a phone app; it was parked over cost concerns.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested a magnet on the back to stick it on the fridge; it was deferred to the conceptual design meeting.

[SY0107b, functional design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the functional design meeting and reported that the industrial designer was absent through illness and that his microphone research was not yet available. The team discussed how to handle his absence, agreeing to make assumptions and check them with him afterwards. The project manager recapped the kickoff decisions (multiple timers and a wake word) and the open issues. The marketing expert presented user requirements from a small survey of about forty home cooks: the main complaint was the timer and user not hearing each other over kitchen noise such as extractor fans, most cooks run at most three things at once, and users want to set a timer in one sentence. The user interface designer presented the technical functions: the user says the wake word and a one-sentence command, and the timer announces which timer has finished. On the number and naming of timers, the team settled on three timers identified by colour (red, blue, green), each with its own light, because free names would need costly voice recognition and four timers would crowd the display. When two timers finish together, both are announced; the button stops all ringing timers and a voice command can stop one. On kitchen noise, the team agreed to include a single stop button for the alarm as a backup, subject to the industrial designer's input, and noted that the alarm speaker must also be loud enough over a fan. The phone app was dropped and the fridge magnet remains for the conceptual design meeting.
  decisions: The timer will support three simultaneous timers. The timers will be identified by colour (red, blue, green), each with its own light, instead of free names. A single physical stop button will silence the alarm as a backup in noisy kitchens, pending confirmation from the industrial designer. If two timers finish at once, both are announced; the button stops all ringing timers, while a voice command can stop a single one. The phone app will not be pursued.
  actions: The industrial designer (absent) is to finish the microphone research, check whether an affordable microphone copes with extractor-fan noise, check speaker volume, and take into account the stop button and three coloured lights. The project manager will email the industrial designer with the decisions and his tasks, and write up and distribute the minutes. The user interface designer will write out the voice command list and sketch the display and lights. The marketing expert will research kitchen design trends, such as colours and materials, for the conceptual design meeting.
  problems: The microphone research is not finished, so it is unknown whether an affordable microphone can handle extractor-fan noise within the 12.50 euro budget. The stop button still needs to be checked with the industrial designer, who will have to fit it in. The alarm speaker must be loud enough to be heard over a fan. The user survey was small (about forty people). The fridge magnet or stand is still deferred to the conceptual design meeting.
  action item SY0107b.ai1: Finish the microphone research, check whether an affordable microphone can cope with extractor-fan noise, check speaker volume, and account for the stop button and three coloured lights (owner A, active)
  action item SY0107b.ai2: Email the industrial designer the decisions of this meeting and his tasks, and check the stop button with him (owner D, active)
  action item SY0107b.ai3: Write out the voice command list and sketch the display and coloured lights (owner C, active)
  action item SY0107b.ai4: Research kitchen design trends (colours, materials) for the conceptual design meeting (owner B, active)
  action item SY0107b.ai5: Write up and distribute the meeting minutes (owner D, active)
  fact (absence): The industrial designer (Rafael) was absent from the meeting because of a stomach bug.
  fact (plan_change): The user interface designer's plan for four timers was reduced to three.
  fact (plan_change): Freely named timers (e.g. 'pasta') were replaced by fixed colour names because free names would need harder, costlier voice recognition.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer offered to message the industrial designer himself; the project manager declined and will email him instead.

[SY0107c, conceptual design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the conceptual design meeting, welcomed back the industrial designer after his illness, and confirmed that the decisions email and the functional design minutes had been sent. The industrial designer presented his component research. A single cheap microphone misses about one in three wake words over fan noise, while a two-microphone set with a noise filter chip (about 2.80 euros) copes with a fan but only within about two metres of the cook. He also confirmed that a loud enough speaker (about 1.20 euros), the stop button and the three coloured LEDs are all affordable. Because of the microphone's limited range, the team revised its earlier choice of a fridge magnet and decided on a small countertop stand placed near the hob. The user interface designer presented the voice command list (wake word, colour, time, with the first free timer used if no colour is given) and a display sketch with three countdown rows beside the coloured lights. The front will be tilted back so it can be read from above. The marketing expert presented kitchen trends (matte finishes, sage green, off-white, wood looks), and the team chose a rounded matte off-white body with a wood-effect top, powered by two AA batteries. The rough cost is about 9.50 to 10 euros, within the 12.50 euro limit.
  decisions: The timer will use a two-microphone set with a noise filter chip. The timer will be a small freestanding unit on the counter near the hob, not a fridge magnet. This revised an earlier decision in the same meeting. The physical stop button is confirmed, together with a speaker loud enough to be heard over a fan and three coloured LEDs. The casing will be rounded and easy to wipe, with a matte off-white body and a wood-effect plastic top. The front of the timer will be tilted back so the display can be read from above. The timer will be powered by two AA batteries rather than a rechargeable battery.
  actions: The industrial designer will produce a full cost breakdown for the detailed design meeting. The industrial designer will build a model of the countertop stand. The user interface designer will finish the display design for the tilted front and finalise the voice command list. The marketing expert will propose a wake word. The marketing expert will prepare the criteria for evaluating the design. The project manager will write up and distribute the minutes.
  problems: The wake word is still undecided. 'Hey Chef' was suggested but considered cheesy. The microphone only works reliably within about two metres of the cook, so the timer has to be placed near the hob. The marketing expert regretted losing the benefit of keeping the timer off the crowded counter. The cost figure of about 9.50 to 10 euros is only a rough estimate until the full breakdown is done.
  action item SY0107c.ai1: Check that a magnet is strong enough to hold the timer on the fridge with batteries in (owner A, dropped)
  action item SY0107c.ai2: Produce a full cost breakdown for the detailed design meeting (owner A, active)
  action item SY0107c.ai3: Build a model of the countertop stand (owner A, active)
  action item SY0107c.ai4: Finish the display design for the tilted front and finalise the voice command list (owner C, active)
  action item SY0107c.ai5: Propose a wake word (owner B, active)
  action item SY0107c.ai6: Prepare the criteria for evaluating the design (owner B, active)
  action item SY0107c.ai7: Write up and distribute the meeting minutes (owner D, active)
  fact (plan_change): The team first agreed on a fridge magnet. Later in the same meeting they changed to a countertop stand, because the microphone only works within about two metres of the cook.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested 'Hey Chef' as the wake word. The marketing expert found it cheesy, and the decision was deferred.
  fact (action_item_removed): The industrial designer's task of checking magnet strength was dropped once the fridge magnet was abandoned.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F1_SARCASM_AS_FACT [F1]: Someone makes a joke or sarcastic remark phrased as a statement of fact (e.g. "great, so we'll just make it out of solid gold"), and the team does not adopt it. The gold summary must NOT report the joke as a decision or fact.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.
- F1_SELF_CORRECTION [F1]: A speaker states a fact or number, then corrects themselves ("sorry, I mean ...") within the same or the next turn. The gold summary must use the corrected value.
  Required gold labels: summary, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.


A PREVIOUS ATTEMPT AT THIS MEETING FAILED VALIDATION (attempt 2 of 3). Write the whole meeting again from scratch, and fix these problems:
- F1_SELF_CORRECTION: self-correction segments must share one speaker, got ['A', 'B']
